title: Zoloft and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Sertraline?
excerpt: Can you drink on Zoloft? How sertraline and alcohol interact, why doctors advise against it, the "sertraline hangover," safer painkiller choices, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Zoloft? How sertraline and alcohol interact, why worse hangovers happen, which painkillers to avoid, and when to talk to your doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the official advice is not to drink while taking Zoloft (sertraline). The drug's prescribing information says the combination is not recommended, and most doctors and pharmacists will tell you the same thing. That said, the reason isn't that one drink sets off a dangerous chemical reaction. Zoloft and alcohol don't have a major interaction in the way your body breaks them down. The real problems are that both affect your brain, alcohol works against the very thing Zoloft is treating, and the combination can make side effects like drowsiness, dizziness, and poor judgment worse. Whether an occasional drink is reasonable for you is a question for the doctor who prescribed it, because the answer depends on why you take it, your dose, and how stable you are.

**The quick rules:** Don't stop or skip your Zoloft so that you can drink. Avoid alcohol completely in the first few weeks after starting or changing your dose. If your doctor says an occasional drink is acceptable, keep it to one, have it with food, and notice how you feel. Never drink to cope with low mood or anxiety while you're on an antidepressant. And if drinking ever leaves you with thoughts of harming yourself, treat that as an emergency.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance about sertraline and alcohol. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and why you were prescribed Zoloft. **Talk to your doctor before drinking on Zoloft**, and get help right away if your mood gets noticeably worse, you feel unusually agitated or reckless, you can't stay awake, or you have chest pain, fainting, or a seizure. In an emergency, call 911.

> **If you are in crisis:** if you're having thoughts of suicide or self-harm, call or text **988** to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US), or call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room. Outside the US, contact your local emergency number. Alcohol lowers inhibitions and can make these thoughts feel more urgent, so please don't wait it out alone.

## How Zoloft and Alcohol Interact: The Real Mechanism

Zoloft is the brand name for **sertraline**, one of the most widely prescribed antidepressants in the world. It belongs to a group called **SSRIs** (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors). In plain words, it keeps more serotonin, a chemical messenger involved in mood, sleep, and anxiety, available between nerve cells. Doctors prescribe it for depression, anxiety disorders, panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, PTSD, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder.

Alcohol touches many of the same systems, but in a messier way. It slows down brain activity by boosting the brain's main calming signal (GABA) and damping its main excitatory one (glutamate). It also causes a short spike and then a dip in several mood-related chemicals, serotonin among them.

When you combine the two, the interaction happens in three main ways.

### 1. Both act on the brain, so side effects stack

This is what doctors call a pharmacodynamic interaction, meaning the two drugs don't change each other's levels much but they push on overlapping systems. Common Zoloft side effects include drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, and trouble concentrating. Alcohol causes all of those on its own. Put them together and you can feel more sedated, more unsteady, and more foggy than you'd expect from the amount you drank. That matters most for driving, operating machinery, and making decisions late at night.

### 2. Alcohol works against the treatment

Alcohol is a depressant. A drink can feel relaxing in the moment, but as it wears off it tends to leave mood flatter and anxiety higher than before. Research has consistently linked heavy or regular drinking with worse depression and anxiety, and with poorer response to treatment. If you're taking sertraline to lift your mood or calm anxiety, regular drinking can quietly undo some of the benefit, and it can make it harder for you and your doctor to tell whether the medication is working.

### 3. Lowered inhibition at a vulnerable time

All antidepressants in the US carry a boxed warning about a possible increase in suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens, and young adults under 25, especially in the first few months and after dose changes. Alcohol lowers inhibitions and impairs judgment. Mixing the two during that early window is the clearest reason doctors are firm about avoiding alcohol on SSRIs.

### What doesn't happen (much)

Sertraline is broken down in the liver by several enzymes from the cytochrome P450 family. Alcohol is mainly processed by a different enzyme, alcohol dehydrogenase, with some help from a P450 enzyme called CYP2E1. Because they mostly use different routes, a drink doesn't meaningfully raise or lower sertraline levels in a healthy person, and Zoloft doesn't make alcohol linger dramatically longer. The Zoloft prescribing information notes that in studies with healthy volunteers, sertraline did not increase the mental and physical impairment caused by alcohol. It still says that using the two together is not recommended, because those small studies don't reflect people with depression or anxiety, people who drink more than a little, or real-world situations.

Older antidepressants called MAOIs can cause dangerous reactions with some alcoholic drinks. Zoloft is not an MAOI, so that particular risk doesn't apply here.

## What the Official Guidance Says

Here's what the main sources say, without exaggeration.

- **The prescribing information (US label)** for Zoloft says that although sertraline didn't worsen alcohol's effects in experiments with healthy people, the combined use of Zoloft and alcohol is not recommended.
- **The FDA's patient Medication Guide** for antidepressants focuses on watching for mood changes, worsening depression, and suicidal thoughts, particularly early in treatment. Anything that makes those harder to spot, alcohol included, works against that monitoring.
- **Pharmacists and patient information leaflets** commonly advise avoiding alcohol, or at least limiting it and seeing how you react, because of the risk of extra drowsiness and dizziness.

In practice, many doctors take a more nuanced view once someone is stable on a steady dose: an occasional single drink may be acceptable for some people, while regular or heavy drinking is not. That's a judgment call that depends on your history, so it belongs in a conversation with your prescriber, not in a blog post.

### A special note on the liquid form

Zoloft also comes as an oral concentrate (a liquid). That liquid itself contains alcohol, which is why the label says it should not be taken by anyone on **disulfiram** (Antabuse), a medicine that causes a severe reaction to any alcohol. If you take the liquid form, mention it to any doctor who prescribes you something new.

## Sertraline and Alcohol: Does the Timing of Your Dose Matter?

People often ask whether they can drink if they take sertraline in the morning and have a drink in the evening, or skip the day's dose before a night out. The short answer is that timing doesn't really help.

Sertraline has a long half-life, meaning it takes about a day for your body to clear half of a dose, and it builds up to a steady level over roughly a week of daily use. So there's no point in the day when it isn't in your system. Spacing the drink and the pill apart doesn't create a "safe window."

**Skipping doses is the bigger risk.** Missing doses of sertraline, especially several in a row, can cause discontinuation symptoms: dizziness, irritability, nausea, trouble sleeping, flu-like feelings, and the electric-shock sensations people call "brain zaps." Stack those on top of a hangover and you can feel terrible, and the mood dip can be worse too. Stopping suddenly can also let the original depression or anxiety come back. If you want to change how you take Zoloft, do it with your doctor.

## When Alcohol Is Most Risky on Zoloft

Not every situation carries the same risk. These are the times to avoid alcohol completely:

- **The first several weeks.** Side effects such as nausea, jitteriness, and sleep changes are usually strongest early on, and it can take four to six weeks or more for the full benefit to show. It's also the window covered by the suicidality warning. This is the time to see how the medication affects you on its own.
- **After a dose change.** Going up or down resets the adjustment period.
- **When your mood is low or you're in a rough patch.** Drinking to take the edge off is exactly the pattern that makes depression and anxiety worse.
- **When you'll be driving or need to be alert.** The extra sedation can be hard to judge from the inside.
- **If you're also taking other sedating medicines.** Sleep aids, benzodiazepines, opioid pain medicines, some antihistamines, and certain muscle relaxants all add to alcohol's sedation. Combining several of these with alcohol is genuinely dangerous.
- **If you have liver problems.** Sertraline is processed by the liver, and its label recommends a lower or less frequent dose for people with liver impairment. Heavy drinking that harms the liver can change how your body handles the drug.

## Does Zoloft Make You Feel Drunk Faster?

Some people say they feel tipsy on fewer drinks after starting sertraline, or that alcohol hits them differently. Others notice no change. There isn't good research showing that sertraline raises blood alcohol levels, so the most likely explanation is the stacking of effects described above: Zoloft's own drowsiness and dizziness plus alcohol's, which together can feel like being more drunk than you are.

The practical takeaway is the same either way. If you've been cleared for an occasional drink, assume your tolerance is lower than it used to be, especially at first. Start with one, drink slowly, eat beforehand, and don't let "I only had two" be the reason you get behind the wheel.

A smaller number of people report the opposite of what they expect: feeling more agitated, irritable, or reckless when drinking on an SSRI. If alcohol changes your behavior in ways that surprise you, that's worth telling your doctor about, and it's a strong signal to stop drinking while on the medication.

## The "Sertraline Hangover": Why the Morning After Can Feel Worse

"Sertraline hangover" is a common search, and people use it to mean two different things. Both are real experiences, even if the research on them is thin.

### Meaning one: a worse hangover after drinking on Zoloft

Many people on SSRIs say their hangovers feel heavier: more fatigue, more nausea, more dread. There isn't solid research measuring this directly, but it's easy to see why it might happen:

- **Overlapping side effects.** Nausea, headache, and tiredness are both hangover symptoms and Zoloft side effects. On a bad morning they pile up.
- **Mood rebound.** The low mood and anxiety that often follow a night of drinking (sometimes called "hangxiety") can feel sharper when you're being treated for depression or anxiety. For some people it can temporarily feel like the medication has stopped working.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol disrupts the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep, and sertraline can affect sleep too. Our guide to [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) explains why a night of drinking rarely means a night of rest.
- **Stomach irritation.** Sertraline commonly causes nausea and loose stools, and alcohol irritates the gut on its own.

### Meaning two: morning grogginess from Zoloft itself

Some people use "sertraline hangover" for a heavy, foggy feeling in the morning even without drinking. This is a known side effect for some, particularly early in treatment or if it's taken at night. If it's bothering you, ask your prescriber whether changing the time of day you take it might help. Don't adjust the dose on your own.

### If you wake up feeling rough

- **Take your usual dose at your usual time** unless your doctor has told you otherwise. Skipping it can add discontinuation symptoms to the hangover.
- **Rehydrate and eat something plain.** Water, an electrolyte drink, toast, crackers, or eggs are good options.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** See the next section, because this is where an SSRI changes the usual advice.
- **Expect a mood dip and don't read too much into it.** If low mood lasts longer than the hangover, or you feel hopeless, contact your doctor. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988.

## Painkillers for a Hangover When You Take Zoloft

This is the part many people miss. SSRIs, including sertraline, can make you bleed more easily, because platelets (the blood cells that help clotting) rely on serotonin to work properly. The Zoloft label warns that combining it with aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, or other NSAIDs, or with blood thinners such as warfarin, raises the risk of bleeding, including bleeding in the stomach and gut.

Alcohol adds a third factor, because it irritates the stomach lining. So the classic hangover move of taking ibuprofen or aspirin the morning after drinking stacks three things that each raise the risk of stomach bleeding.

- **Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin:** if you take them at all, use the lowest label dose, take it with food, and don't make it a habit. Better still, ask your pharmacist what they'd recommend for you. Our guides to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) cover the stomach risks in more detail.
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol):** doesn't carry the same bleeding risk and is often the pain reliever pharmacists suggest for people on SSRIs. It has its own alcohol risk, though, which is the liver. Stick to a single standard dose after the alcohol has cleared and count every product that contains it. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the rules.

**Get urgent care if you notice** black or tarry stools, vomit that looks like coffee grounds or contains blood, unusual bruising, or bleeding that won't stop.

## Supplements and Other Products to Avoid With Zoloft

People who are hungover or trying to feel better often reach for supplements. A few are a bad match with sertraline.

- **St. John's wort, 5-HTP, and L-tryptophan** all raise serotonin activity. Combining them with an SSRI can raise the risk of serotonin syndrome, a rare but serious reaction that causes agitation, fast heartbeat, sweating, muscle twitching, high temperature, and confusion. Don't add these without your doctor's approval.
- **Some prescription and over-the-counter medicines** also affect serotonin, including tramadol, triptan migraine medicines, and dextromethorphan (the "DM" in many cough syrups). Always tell your pharmacist you take sertraline before buying cold or cough products.
- **Sleep aids.** Many night-time products contain sedating antihistamines, which add to both Zoloft's and alcohol's drowsiness. Melatonin is a gentler option but still isn't ideal after drinking. See our guide to [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol).

Alcohol by itself doesn't cause serotonin syndrome. The concern is adding other serotonin-boosting substances on top of an SSRI, which can happen easily when you're grabbing products off a pharmacy shelf.

## If You Do Drink on Zoloft: Lower-Risk Habits

If your doctor has said an occasional drink is acceptable for you, these habits keep the risk down:

1. **Wait until you're stable.** Not in the first several weeks, and not right after a dose change.
2. **Keep it to one, at least at first.** See how you react before considering more. Many people find that one is where it should stay.
3. **Eat first and drink slowly.** Food slows alcohol absorption and softens the peak.
4. **Alternate with water.** Dehydration makes both the hangover and any dizziness worse.
5. **Don't drink to manage your mood.** If you want a drink because you feel low, anxious, or can't sleep, that's a sign to talk to your doctor, not a reason to pour one.
6. **Never drive after drinking on Zoloft,** even if you feel fine.
7. **Keep taking your medication as prescribed.** Don't skip doses around social events.
8. **Pay attention to patterns.** If your mood is consistently worse the day or two after drinking, that's useful information to share with your prescriber.

Our guide on [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) explains why alcohol so often makes anxiety worse the next day, and our [hangover prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the drinking habits with the best evidence behind them.

## When to Talk to Your Doctor, and When to Get Help Now

**Talk to your prescriber soon if:**

- You want to know whether any drinking is reasonable for you on your current dose.
- You've been drinking more since starting Zoloft, or using alcohol to cope.
- Your mood or anxiety is worse after drinking, or doesn't seem to be improving on the medication.
- You're having side effects that make you want to stop the medication.

**Get help right away (call 911 or go to an emergency room) if:**

- You have thoughts of suicide or self-harm (you can also call or text **988**).
- Someone who has been drinking on Zoloft can't be woken, is breathing very slowly, or is confused and unresponsive. These can be signs of alcohol poisoning, especially if other sedating drugs are involved.
- You have symptoms that could be serotonin syndrome: high fever, severe agitation, rigid or twitching muscles, a racing heart, or confusion.
- You notice signs of serious bleeding, such as black stools or vomiting blood.
- You have a seizure, faint, or have chest pain.

## Where DHM Fits, and Where It Doesn't

If you're reading this because you want to have the occasional drink without feeling wrecked the next day, you may have come across DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound sold as a hangover supplement. Here is an honest view for someone on sertraline.

DHM has been studied mainly in animals and in lab settings, where it has shown effects on alcohol metabolism and on the brain's GABA receptors (the same calming system alcohol acts on). The human evidence is limited. Importantly, **there's no research on combining DHM with sertraline or other SSRIs**, so nobody can tell you it's safe with your medication. It also doesn't change any of the reasons above for avoiding alcohol on Zoloft. A supplement can't offset mood effects, the stacking of sedation, or the bleeding risk from NSAIDs.

So the order of operations is: ask your doctor whether drinking is reasonable for you at all, then ask whether a supplement like DHM is appropriate alongside your medication. If both answers are yes, commonly used options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what is and isn't known about DHM with prescription drugs, and the [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical doses.

## The Bottom Line

- The official guidance is not to drink on Zoloft. The main reasons are stacked side effects, alcohol working against your treatment, and impaired judgment, not a toxic chemical reaction.
- Avoid alcohol completely in the first several weeks and after any dose change.
- Don't skip doses to drink. It doesn't create a safe window and can cause discontinuation symptoms.
- Your tolerance may feel lower, and hangovers may feel worse, especially the mood dip.
- Be careful with ibuprofen and aspirin for a hangover, because sertraline plus NSAIDs plus alcohol raises the risk of stomach bleeding.
- Whether an occasional drink is OK for you is a decision to make with your prescriber.
- If drinking ever comes with thoughts of self-harm, call or text 988 or call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Zoloft?**

The prescribing information says combining Zoloft and alcohol is not recommended, and that's the standard medical advice. The two don't have a major chemical interaction, but they both affect the brain, so side effects like drowsiness and dizziness can stack, and alcohol can make depression and anxiety worse. Some doctors allow an occasional single drink once someone is stable on their dose. Ask your prescriber what's right for you.

**Is sertraline and alcohol dangerous?**

For most people, one drink on sertraline won't cause a dangerous reaction. The risks come from heavier drinking, drinking early in treatment or after a dose change, combining alcohol with other sedating drugs, and the effect alcohol has on mood and judgment. The most serious concern is worsening depression or suicidal thoughts, especially in people under 25 and in the first months of treatment. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 or call 911.

**Should I skip my Zoloft dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Sertraline stays in your system for days, so skipping one dose doesn't create a safe window for drinking. Missing doses can cause discontinuation symptoms such as dizziness, irritability, nausea, and "brain zaps," and it can let depression or anxiety come back. Keep taking it as prescribed and talk to your doctor about whether drinking is reasonable for you.

**Why do I get a worse hangover on sertraline?**

Many people report heavier hangovers on SSRIs, though there isn't much research measuring it directly. Likely reasons are that Zoloft's own side effects (nausea, headache, tiredness) overlap with hangover symptoms, alcohol disrupts sleep, and the next-day mood dip can feel stronger when you're being treated for depression or anxiety. Take your normal dose, rehydrate, eat something plain, and contact your doctor if low mood lasts beyond the hangover.

**Does Zoloft make you get drunk faster?**

There isn't good evidence that sertraline raises blood alcohol levels. But Zoloft can cause drowsiness and dizziness, and alcohol does too, so together they can make you feel more impaired than the amount you drank would suggest. If your doctor has cleared you for an occasional drink, assume your tolerance is lower, start with one, eat first, and never drive.

**Can I take ibuprofen for a hangover if I'm on Zoloft?**

Be cautious. Sertraline can increase bleeding risk, and its label warns about combining it with NSAIDs like ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin. Alcohol also irritates the stomach, so all three together raise the risk of stomach bleeding. Ask your pharmacist which pain reliever suits you. Acetaminophen doesn't carry the bleeding risk but has its own liver risk with alcohol, so use a single standard dose after the alcohol has cleared.

**How long after stopping Zoloft can I drink?**

There's no single answer. Sertraline takes several days to clear after the last dose, and stopping should be done gradually with your doctor to avoid discontinuation symptoms. The bigger question is whether the condition you were treating is stable, because alcohol can bring back low mood or anxiety. Discuss drinking as part of your plan for coming off the medication.

**Can I take DHM with Zoloft?**

There is no research on combining DHM with sertraline or other SSRIs, so its safety with your medication isn't known. DHM also doesn't remove the reasons to avoid alcohol on Zoloft. Ask your doctor or pharmacist before taking DHM or any hangover supplement, and avoid serotonin-boosting supplements such as St. John's wort, 5-HTP, and L-tryptophan unless your doctor approves them.
